relevant_findings: Residential repaint walls require condition-based prep that differs significantly from new construction.
Previously painted surfaces in good condition need minimal prep: light sand/scuff, spot prime nail holes.
Fair condition surfaces require more extensive prep: fill cracks, repair dings, prime stains/repairs.
Edge work (cut-in) is LF-based and typically freehand in residential repaint unless premium finish required.
Tape-line edge strategy used when color contrast is high or homeowner expects crisp lines.
Residential environments require furniture/floor protection and careful access management.
Occupied homes have scheduling constraints and ventilation requirements.
condition_drivers: Surface condition: good (minor wear) vs fair (moderate repairs needed).
Presence of stains, water damage, or smoke damage requiring specialty primers.
Color change magnitude: light-to-light vs dark-to-light vs light-to-dark.
Sheen selection: matte/eggshell more forgiving than satin/semi-gloss.
Room complexity: number of corners, windows, doors affecting edge LF.
quality_differences: QL-3: Standard residential - two coats, basic cut-in, minimal sanding between coats.
QL-4: Enhanced residential - light sand between coats, tighter cut lines, inspection pass.
QL-5: Premium residential - full sand/inspect between coats, tape-line edges, zero visible defects.
failure_modes: Adhesion failure over glossy or contaminated existing paint.
Bleed-through of stains, knots, or water damage without proper spot priming.
Lap marks and roller stipple inconsistency.
Uneven sheen from insufficient film build or poor wet-edge management.
Ragged cut lines from dull brushes or poor technique.
Tape bleed when using tape-line strategy on textured surfaces.
Color uniformity issues with deep/saturated colors requiring additional coats.
notes_for_materials_manager: Include stain-blocking primer for spot priming repairs and stains.
Standard interior latex for walls; consider low-VOC for occupied spaces.
Brush quality matters more for freehand cut-in than tape-line strategy.
Account for roller cover changes between primer touch-up and finish coats.
Fair condition increases spackle, caulk, and sandpaper consumption.
notes_for_sop_librarian: Model prep as condition-dependent: good condition = light prep module, fair = extended prep module.
Edge work as LF tasks: freehand cut-in OR tape apply/cut-to-tape/tape remove.
Field coats as SF tasks: roll prime (if needed), roll coat 1, roll coat 2.
Include protection setup/teardown as fixed tasks.
Quality rounds affect sanding/inspection between coats, not coat count.
notes_for_estimation_engineer: Wall SF from PaintScope: room perimeter × wall height minus openings.
Edge LF from PaintScope: ceiling line LF + baseboard line LF + opening casing LF.
Prep rates vary significantly between good and fair condition - model as separate rate sets.
Freehand cut-in is slower per LF than tape-line cut-to-tape but has no tape material cost.
Protection setup is more time-intensive in residential (furniture, floors) than NC.
assumptions: Existing paint is latex or compatible coating; lead paint testing out of scope.
Walls are structurally sound; major drywall repair is excluded.
Homeowner provides access; work area will be clear or clearing is included.
Standard ceiling height (8-10ft); high ceilings require access factor.
Production rates are placeholders pending field calibration.
uncertainties: Actual time difference between good vs fair condition prep needs field validation.
Freehand cut-in rates vary widely by painter skill level.
Deep color coverage may require third coat - not modeled in base spec.
